name: Musa Cafe — POS + Website
tagline: Full restaurant stack: customer website, staff POS, and admin — with a Go backend built for live shop operations.
description:
Musa Cafe is production restaurant software, not a toy demo. Customers order from a website, staff run the counter through a POS, and owners manage the business from an admin dashboard — all backed by a shared Go API so online and in-store orders stay on one system of record.

The POS is built for real service conditions: orders, printing, history, analytics, and offline-capable flows so the counter can keep moving when the network blips. This is shop software used in live restaurant operations.

problem: Independent restaurants often run a website for online orders, a separate POS at the counter, and no unified admin view. Orders get lost between systems, printing and kitchen flow break under pressure, and owners lack a single source of truth for sales and history.
approach: One Go backend serving three purpose-built frontends: a customer ordering site, a staff POS optimized for speed and offline resilience, and an admin dashboard for products, orders, and analytics. Every order path writes through the same API.
solution: A full restaurant stack where website orders and counter sales land in one system. Staff get POS workflows for orders, printing, and history; admins get operational controls and analytics; the Go API keeps the business synchronized across locations.
outcome: Live shop software in active restaurant use — handling real customer orders from website to kitchen, with POS and admin workflows built for day-to-day operations.
features: Customer-facing website for browsing and online ordering
Staff POS for counter orders, tickets, and fast checkout
Admin dashboard for catalog, orders, and business oversight
Offline-capable POS flows for unreliable networks
Order printing and kitchen-facing operational handoff
Order history and sales analytics for owners
architecture: Three Next.js frontends (website, POS, admin) on a shared Go (Gin) REST API and PostgreSQL. Order, product, and sales workflows are centralized so online and in-store channels stay synchronized; POS clients are designed to keep working through brief connectivity issues.
